caption: Figure 1: Tree Ensemble Model. The final prediction for a given example is the sum of predictions from each tree.
description:
Figure type: Diagram showing a tree ensemble model.
Description: The figure displays two decision trees (tree1 and tree2) used in an ensemble model. Each tree predicts a value based on specific conditions. Tree1 predicts based on age and gender, while tree2 predicts based on computer usage. The final prediction is the sum of the predictions from both trees.

caption: Figure 2: Structure Score Calculation. We only need to sum up the gradient and second order gradient statistics on each leaf, then apply the scoring formula to get the quality score.
description:
This figure illustrates the structure score calculation in the XGBoost algorithm. It shows a decision tree with five instances, each assigned a gradient statistic. The tree splits based on age and gender, leading to different leaf nodes. The figure calculates the score for each leaf using gradient and second-order gradient statistics, applying a scoring formula to determine the quality of the structure.

description:

caption: Figure 6: Block structure for parallel learning. Each column in a block is sorted by the corresponding feature value. A linear scan over one column in the block is sufficient to enumerate all the split points.
description:
This figure illustrates the block structure for parallel learning in XGBoost, showing how data is organized and processed. It consists of three main parts: the layout transformation of a single feature column, the input layout of three feature columns, and the linear scan over presorted columns to find the best split. The figure demonstrates how sorting and indexing are used to efficiently compute gradient statistics and identify optimal split points for tree boosting.

caption: Figure 5: Impact of the sparsity aware algorithm on Allstate-10K. The dataset is sparse mainly due to one-hot encoding. The sparsity aware algorithm is more than 50 times faster than the naive version that does not take sparsity into consideration.
description:

The x-axis represents the number of threads, ranging from 1 to 16. The y-axis represents the time per tree in seconds, ranging from 0.03125 to 32. The "Basic algorithm" is represented by a red line with markers, while the "Sparsity aware algorithm" is represented by a blue line with markers. The "Sparsity aware algorithm" is significantly faster than the "Basic algorithm", with a difference of more than 50 times.

caption: Figure 11: Comparison of out-of-core methods on different subsets of criteo data. The missing data points are due to out of disk space. We can find that basic algorithm can only handle 200M examples. Adding compression gives 3x speedup, and sharding into two disks gives another 2x speedup. The system runs out of file cache start from 400M examples. The algorithm really has to rely on disk after this point. The compression+shard method has a less dramatic slowdown when running out of file cache, and exhibits a linear trend afterwards.

caption: Figure 13: Scaling of XGBoost with different number of machines on criteo full 1.7 billion dataset. Using more machines results in more file cache and makes the system run faster, causing the trend to be slightly super linear. XGBoost can process the entire dataset using as little as four machines, and scales smoothly by utilizing more available resources.
description:
Description: This figure is a line graph showing the scaling of XGBoost with different numbers of machines on the Criteo full 1.7 billion dataset. The x-axis represents the number of machines, ranging from 4 to 32. The y-axis represents the time per iteration in seconds, ranging from 128 to 2048. The graph shows a downward trend, indicating that using more machines results in faster processing times.

Description: The graph shows a single line with data points at 4, 8, 16, and 32 machines. The highest point is at 4 machines with a time per iteration of approximately 2048 seconds. The lowest point is at 32 machines with a time per iteration of approximately 128 seconds. The trend is slightly super linear, indicating that using more machines results in more file cache and faster processing times.
